## What's new

Threadnote 5 turns engineering context into a trustworthy lifecycle. Once Threadnote is connected, a supported agent
automatically starts non-trivial work with a short brief grounded in the current source, continues with the current code
as the authority, and closes out with a private handoff plus a reviewable proposal for anything worth preserving.
Approved knowledge can then help another agent, while health checks make stale or conflicting context visible before it
causes confusion.

The lifecycle is local-first and works across supported coding-agent environments. Personal work stays on your machine;
nothing becomes shared knowledge merely because an agent saw it. Threadnote keeps the decision to save, edit, share, or
retire context with you.

### Setup: connect Threadnote to an agent

Choose an agent environment from the catalog, preview the setup plan, and apply it when it looks right:

```sh
threadnote agents list
threadnote setup <surface>
threadnote setup <surface> --apply
```

Here, a _surface_ means one supported coding-agent environment and its local project-integration files. Setup prepares
Threadnote for the current repository, installs or repairs the selected integration, builds the code evidence it needs,
runs checks, and installs the concise lifecycle instructions that tell the agent when to use a Context Brief, verify code,
and close out its work. Setup finishes by producing a real Context Brief. Preview is read-only. An interrupted apply can
resume, and undo is preview-first and removes only unchanged files that this setup created. Repeating an already
completed, unchanged setup does not duplicate the work.

The final verification uses a built-in repository-orientation task, so setup does not need a task prompt from you.
Future work receives a fresh brief for the actual task automatically through the installed lifecycle instructions.

Everything in this workflow runs locally. Setup does not silently publish your work. If a catalog entry is not yet
managed automatically, Threadnote explains the manual steps instead of pretending that setup is complete.

### Brief: start with the right context

A **Context Brief** is the small starting packet an agent receives for a task. It combines relevant decisions and
handoffs with compatible, reviewed procedures and evidence from the current code. It says where each piece came from,
how current it is, and when evidence is unavailable or incomplete. After setup, the installed instructions tell the
agent to create this brief automatically for non-trivial work and to verify consequential claims in the files it changes.
You do not need to request the brief in every prompt. This gives the agent a useful starting point without treating an
old chat, memory entry, or vendor-specific store as the source of truth.

For a repository that spans several related projects, define a **Workset**: a named group of repositories that should be
considered together. Worksets make cross-repository discovery explicit. Create or edit the membership, then prepare it
when you want current code evidence published for that group. Changing a definition does not unexpectedly rebuild code;
preparation is the deliberate refresh step. You can inspect readiness before the agent builds its brief.

```sh
threadnote workset create checkout --project api --project web
threadnote workset prepare checkout
```

### Focus a large monorepo on the code your project actually uses

In a large monorepo, one team usually owns only a few applications and the libraries those applications depend on.
Threadnote can now give each project its own dependency-aware code graph instead of indexing every unrelated package.
Choose one or more application or library roots, and Threadnote follows their declared forward dependencies. You can
also include exceptional paths that are required at runtime but are not represented by the workspace dependency model.

Preview the selection before building it:

```sh
threadnote graph scope set storefront --root apps/storefront
threadnote graph scope preview storefront
threadnote graph index --project storefront
```

The preview explains which components and files are included, why dependencies were selected, and whether Threadnote
has a complete enough dependency model to make authoritative negative claims. Query results carry the same coverage,
so an out-of-scope path is reported as outside this project's graph rather than incorrectly described as missing.

Once the scope is active, changes to unrelated applications and packages do not make this graph stale or consume a
builder slot. Ordinary edits inside the project use incremental indexing, compatible overlapping scopes reuse proven
work, and linked worktrees keep their dirty source and active views isolated. A configured scope also follows the
project into a linked worktree, including when Threadnote refreshes source evidence for an agent's Context Brief.
Workspace discovery understands commented JSON configuration, TypeScript path aliases, nested Node layouts, and Bazel
packages, while keeping harmless metadata diagnostics from obscuring an otherwise usable scope. Changing a dependency
manifest updates the selected closure when necessary. Projects without a graph scope continue to use the full
repository, and clearing the scope is the explicit full-graph fallback:

```sh
threadnote graph scope clear storefront --confirm
threadnote graph index --project storefront
```

This removes the need to carry a personal ignore file into every new worktree while keeping the selected graph
reviewable and reproducible.

In Threadnote Manager, use **Edit Project** to configure and preview a scope. The preview shows its progress and then
the selected projects, files, and diagnostics, so you can verify the boundary before you ask Threadnote to index it.

### Work: use current code and reviewed guidance

Threadnote treats the current checkout as authoritative. Historical context can explain why something exists, but it
cannot override what the files say now. Code-relationship discovery helps an agent find connections across the
repository and a Workset, while limited results make missing or incomplete evidence visible instead of silently guessing.

Existing project guidance can now enter this lifecycle too. Import it for review, rather than writing it directly into
saved knowledge:

```sh
threadnote guidance import <surface> --project <name>
threadnote guidance import <surface> --project <name> --apply
```

The first command previews what Threadnote found; `--apply` creates or reuses the private proposal. Review it before
applying anything. When you approve saved knowledge,
you can project selected items into the agent's native project instructions:

```sh
threadnote guidance project <surface> --project <name> --memory <uri>
threadnote guidance project <surface> --project <name> --memory <uri> --apply
```

The first command previews the managed section; `--apply` writes it. Projection keeps that Threadnote-maintained section
separate from text you own. It uses stable ordering
and records which approved knowledge supplied the section. If somebody edits or removes it, status and health checks
report the drift; Threadnote does not silently overwrite the surrounding instructions. Multiple agent environments can
use the same approved knowledge without creating competing source copies.

### Review: turn work into a Knowledge Delta

At closeout, the installed lifecycle tells the agent to record a private handoff automatically. When the task produced
reusable knowledge, the agent also prepares a **Knowledge Delta**: a proposed change to the context available for future
work. Think of it as a reviewable summary of what this task changed in your understanding, not an automatic memory write.

A delta explains, in plain language:

- the decisions made and why they were made;
- constraints or assumptions that future work must respect;
- what was actually checked or verified;
- knowledge that is no longer valid; and
- unresolved risks or questions.

Each proposed item includes the evidence behind it, a recommendation, and the exact change that would be made. You can
approve it, edit it, defer it, or reject it. Personal handoffs and preferences can remain local. If a saved item should
be reused by another person or agent, share it through your normal reviewed Git workflow after approval.

No special closeout prompt is required: the agent follows the installed instructions and presents the delta before
applying any proposed durable knowledge. This separation is the heart of 5.0: the agent discovers and proposes context,
but a person decides what becomes a saved fact.

### Reuse: carry approved knowledge to the next task

Approved saved knowledge can be recalled in later Context Briefs, projected into another supported agent's project
guidance, or deliberately shared through a reviewed Git repository. The original evidence and review decision travel
with the item, so a later agent can see why it was trusted and whether it still needs review.

For teams that want to prove this handoff end to end, **guided two-agent activation** is an optional follow-on to the
normal one-agent setup. It walks one supported agent through a cited brief and reviewed decision, pauses at every import,
save, and sharing boundary, then asks a second configured agent to retrieve that exact approved decision. The proof is
performed by the second agent's own Threadnote connection rather than by pasted output, so it demonstrates that the
shared context is genuinely portable. The journey is resumable, works locally with a Git-backed team share, and does
not require a hosted organization service.

Start from the included request example, preview the journey, and apply it when the selected agents, repositories, and
publication mode look right:

```sh
cp docs/examples/threadnote-activation-request.json /tmp/threadnote-activation.json
threadnote activate start --request /tmp/threadnote-activation.json
threadnote activate start --request /tmp/threadnote-activation.json --apply
```

Threadnote prints the exact continuation or approval needed at each boundary. The final step is completed from the
second agent environment, after which activation records a content-free retrieval receipt. This is an integration proof
for teams, not a prerequisite for normal use; the everyday lifecycle still begins with one connected agent. See the
[guided activation guide](https://threadnote.io/docs/threadnote-5-journey/) for the request fields,
direct-versus-proposal sharing, retrieval proof, and safe undo flow.

Threadnote 5 also accepts **verified procedures** alongside factual knowledge. A procedure is a reviewed, versioned
workflow—for example, a repository operation with a known artifact and checks—not an instruction that Threadnote
downloads and runs on its own. Verify a local procedure with a preview first:

```sh
threadnote procedure verify <manifest> --json
threadnote procedure verify <manifest> --apply --json
```

The first command previews the procedure; the second performs the verification run. Supplied test files can check it.
Status tells you
whether the procedure is current, incompatible, locally modified, unverified, or has an available update. A Context
Brief includes only procedures relevant to the task and supported by complete verification evidence. Nothing untrusted
executes automatically.

### Maintain: keep context useful as code changes

Context is only helpful while it remains connected to reality. Open Threadnote Manager's context-health view to find
expired or overdue knowledge, changed or missing code citations, broken relationships, duplicates, contradictions, and
guidance drift. Health proposes repairs for your review; it does not silently delete, rewrite, renew, or supersede a
record. Unknown code coverage remains unknown instead of being reported as healthy.

Large projects do not have to review every finding at once. Narrow the view to the kind of knowledge, topic, or issue
you are working on, continue through the results in stable pages, and preview repairs for that same scope. If the
underlying context changes while you are reviewing it, Threadnote stops the continuation instead of combining results
from different states. Every proposed repair remains review-only until you approve it.

The new **Context Check** is a local check that also fits automated build and review jobs. It compares the current
checkout with a Git baseline and looks for affected citations, code relationships, active conflicts, documentation gaps,
and places where changed code may need a new capture. It can print text, JSON, or SARIF, a standard format for code-host
annotations:

```sh
threadnote context check --project <name> --base origin/main --format sarif
```

Exit status `0` means the check found no actionable issue with complete evidence; `1` means an actionable finding exists;
`2` means the check could not establish the evidence it needs. Treat `2` as unknown or failed, not as clean. The output
contains limited findings and stable identifiers, not saved text or source excerpts.

The memory format in Threadnote 5 (schema v5) supports optional ownership, a review date, and an expiry date. Ownership
says who should look after a piece of knowledge; review and expiry say when it needs another look or should no longer be
treated as current. These fields support safe lifecycle transitions without changing the meaning or authority of a
record. Existing records remain readable, and migration adds no invented owner or date. Health can surface records that
need attention, while you decide whether to keep, edit, replace, archive, or retire them.

Threadnote also records lightweight, local feedback about recall. Mark a result useful, wrong, pin it, dismiss it, or mark
it applied when it materially informed a plan or change. To inspect the aggregate, run `threadnote value report`. The
local value report summarizes counts such as Context Brief activity, feedback, Knowledge Delta outcomes, health work,
and setup completion. It contains no queries, memory text, source code, paths, repository names, or raw logs, and it does
not upload telemetry. Use it to understand whether context is helping and where it needs improvement; keeping and
deleting the local records remain explicit actions.

### Local and background behavior

Code-relationship indexes and storage cleanup are coordinated across local Threadnote processes. Interactive work keeps
its priority, background work waits fairly, and agents can continue using the last complete index while a fresh one is
being built—unless a task explicitly requires evidence from the latest code. Cleanup retries after active builds finish
and yields rather than competing with foreground work. These background tasks stay on the machine and do not turn
private context into an upload.

That gives 5.0 a complete loop: set up once, let the agent begin with a cited brief and work from current code, review
the Knowledge Delta it proposes at closeout, reuse only what you approved, and maintain it as the codebase changes.
